name: Emeka Evans

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers, unions, AI firms or government. Your answers stay confidential. What do you do on a normal day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Emeka Evans, 58, a junior lineworker at the electricity company after working as a building porter. I hold a vocational certificate, load the truck, help build and repair power lines and ask a mentor to inspect unfamiliar joints; I like restoring a street, but I still find storm calls exhausting.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What is the part you most want to get better at?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Splices that look sound until the clamp comes off. My mentor Anika makes me describe what I see before she shows me the fault, which sticks longer than a screen answer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now let's talk about AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew the work order might get shorter, but the line still has to be safe before a hand goes near it. I'm happy to lose a bit of typing after a long call.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, a quiet change gives me time to catch up on the field skills I entered late. I earn a good rate and have about nine months of household costs saved, so I don't fear a minor paperwork shortcut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep working my assigned line repairs and use the approved text assistant now and then to tidy my end-of-day notes. In the first year I'd keep my normal savings transfer and ask my mentor to check my splice work before signing it off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel at ease about the pay and glad the day still has a clear shape. My partner and our grown children don't need me to invent a new career over a faster form.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you never put into the assistant?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I wouldn't put a customer's private details or a switching instruction into a public tool. The company version only gets my rough wording after the work is finished.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How did you come to line work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I was a building porter before the certificate, and my mentor Anika still has to slow me down on unfamiliar joints. Higher pay has helped us save, but it hasn't made me senior overnight.

say: I'd say **shorter work orders** could help after long field calls.
I'd remind the crew that **safe isolation** still requires human checks.
think: My **late entry** means I need more supervised splice practice.
Our **nine-month reserve** and higher pay make routine automation manageable.
do: Continue **assigned repairs** and ask Anika to check unfamiliar splices.
Use the **approved text assistant** occasionally for end-of-day notes while maintaining normal savings deposits.
feel: **At ease** about wages and the shape of daily work.
S0.quote: Higher pay has helped us save, but it hasn't made me senior overnight.
fieldNote: Emeka's **occasional AI use** is narrow and follows company privacy rules; he does not delegate switching decisions.
The **nine-month reserve** and higher pay lower pressure, while his junior skill remains a real constraint.

steps.text: Continue assigned repairs and supervised splice practice
Use the approved text assistant for end-of-day notes

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now let's talk about Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the office should let dispatchers test a planning tool before it changes their jobs. Faster bookings may help us reach faults, but we depend on the people who know which road floods.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could lose some overtime if booking gets tighter, even while my base field work survives. Nine months saved gives us room to absorb that, though my partner Lila's café hours are not guaranteed either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I'll ask Anika to walk me through the approved fault-location system after the older crew has tried it. In the first year I'll compare its suggested route with the feeder sheet, and if callout pay slips I'll delay replacing our still-working car.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm interested once a tool proves useful, and uneasy for the dispatchers whose experience is hard to put in a database. I'm not racing to be the first person to trust it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the car delay save?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The old hatchback runs well enough for another year, and a replacement would mean a monthly payment. I'd rather keep that payment out of our budget if extra shifts become scarce.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you know the tool had proved itself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd watch whether it finds the correct feeder on wet-weather calls and ask the experienced crew what it missed. One neat demo in the office isn't enough for me.

say: I'd ask **dispatchers** to test planning software before their roles change.
I'd welcome **faster bookings** if local road and feeder knowledge survives.
think: Tighter booking could reduce my **callout pay** while base repairs remain.
Lila's **café hours** can also change, so our reserve matters.
do: Learn the **approved fault system** after experienced crew members have tested it.
Delay the **car replacement** if callout income falls in the first year.
feel: **Interested** after proof, and uneasy for dispatch colleagues.
S1.quote: One neat demo in the office isn't enough for me.
fieldNote: Emeka sees **base field work** continuing, but recognizes overtime and Lila's variable café hours as near-term income risks.
His **car decision** is a real spending lever; he tests route suggestions against wet-weather calls and feeder records.

steps.text: Learn the approved fault-location system after crew trials
Delay replacing the hatchback if callout income falls

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now let's talk about AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew that 2028 thinking AI would change the plans first, but 2031 is when robots could take line repairs. We need the safety rules in writing before that second date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 63 in 2031, I may still need wages and could be the junior person a company lets go. Nine months saved and many utilities nearby help, but neither guarantees a new employer will take me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd ask our union branch for a meeting on robot certification and paid transition courses. In 2029 I'd enroll in a paid inspection course if offered, and when robots arrive in 2031 I'd apply for inspection posts here and at nearby utilities while keeping any paid crew shifts available.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm anxious about the speed, though I have some room to act. I don't want to pretend that learning inspection automatically means an inspection job exists.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does Lila think of the plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner Lila says we should compare the course timetable with her café shifts before I commit. Our grown daughter lives on her own, so we aren't trying to cover a child's school fees.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask the union to secure?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A recognised certificate, paid time for the course and proper tests before a robot touches a live line. A short demonstration wouldn't tell us how it behaves after three wet nights.

say: I'd distinguish **2028 planning AI** from 2031 robots that could repair lines.
I'd ask for **written robot safety rules** before field deployment.
think: At **63**, I may still need wages when junior field posts shrink.
Our **savings and nearby jobs** help without guaranteeing a new offer.
do: Ask the **union branch** for certification and paid-transition talks now.
Enroll in **paid inspection training** if offered in 2029, then apply for inspection posts when robots arrive.
feel: **Anxious** about timing, with savings and applications giving some control.
S2.quote: Nine months saved and many utilities nearby help, but neither guarantees a new employer will take me.
fieldNote: Emeka ties his **employment risk**, while anticipating earlier planning changes from thinking AI.
His **paid training** condition and actual applications avoid treating a certificate as a guaranteed replacement for field wages.

steps.text: Ask the union for robot certification and paid transition courses
Enroll in the 2029 inspection course if paid time is offered
Apply for inspection jobs here and at nearby utilities in 2031
Keep paid crew shifts while applying for inspection work

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now let's talk about AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell colleagues we have five years to find the faults in a machine before it gets near a conductor. Thinking AI comes in 2031, and repair robots arrive around 2034; one good field trial won't settle the safety question.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll be 66 when the robots arrive, and retirement might be possible if our figures hold. Lila's café hours vary, so I won't count her current wage as a fixed amount forever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'd ask for a written retirement forecast and join the union's field trial group if one forms. In 2032 I'd take a paid certificate in testing robotic line equipment if the employer offers it; in 2034 I'd apply for equipment-inspection shifts if our retirement budget is still short.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel cautious but less squeezed. The extra years let me learn what actually breaks, and they give us time to see whether retirement is affordable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the trial group measure?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd log how often the robot finds corrosion under a clamp and whether a crew has to finish the job. The report should include bad weather, not just clear days.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make retirement affordable?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd include roof repairs and Lila's medicine, and use a conservative figure for her café hours. I'd rather work another year than find out our plan depended on every shift going perfectly.

say: I'd call for **bad-weather trials** before 2034 repair robots work on conductors.
I'd separate **2031 thinking AI** from field robots three years later.
think: Retirement at **66** might work if our income forecast holds.
Lila's **variable café pay** makes a simple retirement sum unreliable.
do: Request a **written forecast** and join a union field trial group if formed.
Take a **paid testing certificate** if offered in 2032, then apply for inspection shifts if needed in 2034.
feel: **Cautious**, with less pressure and more time to test the plan.
S3.quote: I'd rather work another year than find out our plan depended on every shift going perfectly.
fieldNote: Emeka uses the longer runway for **bad-weather evidence**, focused on corrosion and jobs crews must complete after robot failures.
His **retirement decision** accounts for roof and medicine costs and discounts Lila's variable income.

steps.text: Compare a written retirement forecast with household repair and medicine costs
Join the union field trial group if it forms
Take the paid robot-testing certificate in 2032 if offered
Apply for equipment-inspection shifts in 2034 if retirement falls short

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now let's talk about AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell younger workers ten years is long enough to bargain for testing, training and a share in decisions. Thinking AI arrives in 2036, while repair robots arrive in 2039, when I'll be 71.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 71 I hope to have retired from climbing, but that depends on a real forecast, not a birthday. With our savings and my higher wage, I think we can probably set a date before 2039 if Lila's hours and our bills cooperate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd keep earning lineworker wages and get the retirement statement in writing. In 2037 Lila and I would choose a retirement date if the figures cover our costs; in the robot year I'd visit the union meeting with my field notes and help new workers spot the limits of the equipment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel fairly calm about our income in this version. I worry more about the younger crew inheriting machines that haven't been tested in rain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your notes tell them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The corner pole on Orchard Lane has a rotten step hidden by paint. I'd show the new workers the photo and the repair record before anyone trusts a clean digital drawing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you invest in robot equipment yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I don't own a line company. Our savings are for living costs and retirement. I'd rather pay attention to the equipment the utility buys and the rules it follows.

say: I'd seek **worker input** on testing and training over the decade.
I'd tell crews **2039 robots** reach field work when I'll be 71.
think: Retirement before **71** looks plausible, but needs a written forecast.
Our **savings and higher wage** help while Lila's hours remain variable.
do: Keep **paid line shifts** while obtaining a retirement statement.
Choose a **2037 retirement date** if costs are covered and bring field notes to a 2039 union meeting.
feel: **Calm** about likely income, concerned for younger crews' safety.
S4.quote: Our savings are for living costs and retirement.
fieldNote: Emeka views **2039 robots** through likely retirement rather than an immediate threat to his own income.
He rejects a **personal equipment investment** because he does not own the utility; his contribution is practical field evidence.

steps.text: Keep paid line shifts and obtain a written retirement statement
Choose a 2037 retirement date only if household costs are covered
Bring Orchard Lane fault notes to the 2039 union meeting

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most: I could be 63 when repair robots arrive in 2031 and still need the wage. Paid inspection training, a recognised certificate, real vacancies and independent wet-weather safety tests would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who carries the repair when the robot stops halfway through a storm. The answer decides whether crews are being trained for a new job or merely kept until the machine improves.

headlineQuote: The answer decides whether crews are being trained for a new job or merely kept until the machine improves.
portrait: Emeka is a **58-year-old junior lineworker** who entered from building maintenance and still relies on a mentor for unfamiliar joints.
His **nine-month reserve** give room to adapt, while Lila's café hours make household income less certain.
He uses **approved AI tools occasionally** for notes and routes once experienced crews have tested them.
The fast scenario's **2031 repair robots** worry him most; he seeks union safety rules, paid training and actual inspection vacancies.
With more time, he weighs **retirement figures** against roof and medicine costs while continuing paid field work.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** worries him most because repair robots arrive in 2031 while he may still need wages.
whatWouldHelp: He wants **paid inspection training**, a recognised certificate, real vacancies and independent wet-weather tests.
